faqs.a: No. robots.txt is a request, not a lock. Well-behaved crawlers obey it, but it does not hide anything from people or bad bots. Anyone can read your robots.txt, so never use it to hide sensitive URLs. Protect those with passwords instead.
faqs.q: Does robots.txt hide pages from hackers?

faqs.a: A blocked page can still appear in Google's index if other sites link to it; Google just shows the URL without a description. To truly remove a page from results, serve it with a noindex meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header instead.
faqs.q: I blocked a page but it still shows in Google. Why?

faqs.a: Test it in Google Search Console under Settings > robots.txt. It shows exactly which URLs your rules block and flags syntax errors. Always test after uploading, because one wrong slash can block your whole site.
faqs.q: How do I test my robots.txt?

robots-txt-generator.formula:
User-agent: [bot name or *]
Disallow: /path-to-block
Allow: /path-to-allow
Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
Rule: most specific match wins; paths are case-sensitive.
howTo: Add one rule per path: the user agent (* for all bots), allow or disallow, and the path.
Block admin areas, carts, and internal search pages. Keep public content allowed.
Add your sitemap URL so crawlers find it immediately.
Optionally set a crawl delay for polite crawling.
Copy or download robots.txt and upload it to your domain root.
keyFacts: robots.txt is a text file at your domain root that tells search-engine crawlers which pages they may visit.
User-agent: * targets all crawlers. Named agents like Googlebot target one crawler.
Disallow: /admin blocks the /admin path and everything under it for that agent.
Allow explicitly permits paths, useful as an exception inside a blocked area.
The Sitemap: line points crawlers to your XML sitemap for faster discovery.
